newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - CWS gets payment, drops Hambros action.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - CWS gets payment, drops Hambros action.

text.p: The Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) on Monday got a "substantial" financial settlement as it dropped legal action against investment bank Hambros and law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite, sources close to the company said.
CWS, Hambros and Travers all declined to comment on the terms of the deal although CWS said it was "satisfied with the apology."

The unprecedented apology from Hambros chairman Sir Chips Keswick, a prominent figure in the City who had earlier refused to countenance criticism by CWS of the bank's conduct in advising entrepreneur Andrew Regan's Galileo in its attempt to take over CWS, was unreserved and came in a letter to CWS chief Graham Melmoth.

"The purpose of this letter is to offer my personal and the bank's unreserved apology and to assure you that we are taking the appropriate action to ensure that this will not happen again," Sir Chips said in his letter.

Last week, CWS executive Alan Prescott, who has led the institution's internal enquiry into the affair, said the defence of the takeover plan had cost it millions of pounds. He predicted, however, that CWS would not be left "out of pocket".

Hambros later said it was retiring as financial adviser to Galileo and Regan's other company Lanica Trust. It said that after consulting banking regulators, it has begun an enquiry into the affair to be carried out by law firm Norton Rose but declined to comment on the scope or nature of the probe.

Galileo's hostile 1.2 billion pounds ($1.9 billion) bid collapsed last week after CWS took legal action to block the use of information leaked to Regan by CWS executives and the withdrawal of key financial backing.
On Friday, a High Court judge said the case represented a "gross, wilful and disgraceful breach of confidence", adding that the bid had been conducted in an "iniquitous manner".
CWS had originally said it would sue Hambros and Travers Smith because they had "acted in breach of an equitable obligation of confidentiality to CWS".
CWS said the two firms could have no credible grounds for believing that Regan and his partners and advisers had obtained documents about CWS legitimately.
Analysts say the publication of such a letter from a prominent City institution is unprecedented.

"It's possible that letters like this have been written before but I can't recall ever seeing one," said one banking analyst who declined to be named. "There's no doubt that the potential loss of revenue to Hambros stemming from this would far exceed any damages they might have had to pay."

CWS chief Melmoth, who waged a highly effective defence advised by SBC Warburg, had attacked Hambros consistently during the saga, writing to the bank to demand explanations of its conduct on several occasions without drawing any admission from Hambros.

On April 21, Keswick wrote to CWS, "I confirm that we continue to act as Lanica and Galileo's advisers. We appear to have differing views and I do not believe that any further correspondence on the questions you have raised is required."

But in Monday's letter, Keswick says, "Regretfully, I have to say that it is quite clear to me the judgement exercised in Hambros, proceeding in the way that it did, fell well below our standards and those which you were entitled to expect from us."
For Hambros, the letter is a humiliating reversal.
Analysts say Hambros may have felt it had to go along with Regan because the bank has been under pressure to perform better.

Last year, Regent Pacific, an Asian investment fund which owns between three and four percent of Hambros shares, wanted the company to return value to shareholders but did not pursue its case after other shareholders said they were willing to give Keswick the benefit of the doubt and allow time to develop his own strategy.
